prompt: What kind of spectrum do you see when light from a continuous source passes through a cooler gas?

choices.text: An absorption spectrum: dark lines in an otherwise continuous spectrum
An emission spectrum: bright lines on a dark background
choices.why: Bright lines come from a glowing gas seen without a continuous source behind it.

choices.text: A purely continuous spectrum, with no lines
choices.why: The cooler gas absorbs certain wavelengths, leaving dark lines in the continuous spectrum.

choices.text: No spectrum at all
choices.why: Most of the light still passes through; only certain wavelengths are absorbed, giving dark lines.

explanation: An absorption spectrum results when light from a continuous source passes through a cooler gas: it shows a series of dark lines characteristic of the composition of the gas.

prompt: Which of these produces an emission (bright-line) spectrum?

choices.text: A gas at low pressure excited by heat or by collisions with electrons
A glowing incandescent solid
choices.why: An incandescent solid gives a continuous spectrum, like blackbody radiation.

choices.text: A gas at high pressure
choices.why: A gas at high pressure gives a continuous spectrum. A line spectrum needs a gas at low pressure.

choices.text: A cool gas in front of a light bulb
choices.why: That gives an absorption spectrum: dark lines in a continuous spectrum.

explanation: An emission spectrum is produced by a gas at low pressure excited by heat or by collisions with electrons. A continuous spectrum comes from an incandescent solid or a gas at high pressure.

prompt: What are Fraunhofer lines?

choices.text: Dark absorption lines in the spectrum of sunlight
Bright lines given off by a hydrogen lamp
choices.why: Those are emission lines. Fraunhofer lines are dark lines in the Sun's spectrum.

choices.text: The colored bands of a fluorescent light
choices.why: Fraunhofer lines are in sunlight: dark gaps found by Wollaston and studied by Fraunhofer.

choices.text: The lines Balmer used to predict hydrogen's spectrum
choices.why: Balmer worked with hydrogen's emission lines. Fraunhofer lines are dark absorption lines in sunlight.

explanation: Fraunhofer lines are the many thin dark lines in the solar spectrum. They are absorption lines, caused by absorption in the cooler outer layers of the Sun.

prompt: What did Newton conclude from his prism experiments?

choices.text: White light is made up of all the colors of the rainbow
The prism adds color to white light
choices.why: Newton showed the colors were already in white light: a second prism recombined them into white light.

choices.text: Light of a single color changes color when it passes through another prism
choices.why: Newton found the opposite: light of a single color did not change color on refraction.

choices.text: Sunlight contains only red, green and blue light
choices.why: Newton found white light contains all the colors of the rainbow.

explanation: Newton passed sunlight through a prism and then used a second prism to reconstitute white light. He concluded that white light is made up of all the colors of the rainbow, which a prism refracts through slightly different angles.

prompt: Balmer's formula is λ = b n_2^2/(n_2^2 − 4), with b = 364.56 nm. What is the wavelength, in nm, of the line with n_2 = 3?
explanation: λ = (364.56 nm)(3^2)/(3^2 − 4) = (364.56 nm)(9/5) = 656.2 nm. This is the red Hα line of hydrogen.

prompt: According to Table 1.4.2, what color is the Balmer line at 656 nm (n_2 = 3)?

choices.text: Red
Blue
choices.why: The blue line is at 434 nm (n_2 = 5). The 656 nm line is red.

choices.text: Violet
choices.why: Violet lines are near 397–410 nm. The 656 nm line is red.

choices.text: Teal
choices.why: The teal line is at 486 nm (n_2 = 4). The 656 nm line is red.

explanation: Table 1.4.2 lists the 656 nm line (n_2 = 3) as red. It is the longest-wavelength line of the Balmer series, known as hydrogen's Hα line.

prompt: What is a wavenumber, ν̃?

choices.text: The reciprocal of the wavelength, usually in cm^−1
The number of waves in a light beam
choices.why: A wavenumber is defined as 1/λ, usually measured in cm^−1.

choices.text: The wavelength measured in centimeters
choices.why: It is the reciprocal of the wavelength, 1/λ, not the wavelength itself.

choices.text: The speed of light divided by the wavelength
choices.why: c/λ is the frequency ν. The wavenumber is 1/λ = ν/c.

explanation: The wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength, ν̃ = 1/λ = ν/c, usually given in cm^−1.

prompt: Why are wavenumbers convenient in spectroscopy?

choices.text: They are directly proportional to energy (E = hcν̃)
They are always whole numbers
choices.why: Wavenumbers can be any value. They are useful because E = hcν̃.

choices.text: They are inversely proportional to energy
choices.why: It is the wavelength that is inversely proportional to energy. Wavenumber and energy are directly proportional: E = hcν̃.

choices.text: They do not depend on the light at all
choices.why: A wavenumber is a property of the light, 1/λ, and it is proportional to the light's energy.

explanation: E = hc/λ = hcν̃, so the wavenumber is directly proportional to energy, which makes it a convenient unit in spectroscopy.

prompt: Light has a wavelength of 500 nm, which is 5.00 × 10^−5 cm. What is its wavenumber, ν̃ = 1/λ, in cm^−1?
Who first observed the spectrum of hydrogen atoms, in 1853?

choices.text: Anders Ångström
Johann Balmer
choices.why: Balmer later found a formula for the visible lines, using the wavelengths Ångström had measured.

choices.text: Joseph von Fraunhofer
choices.why: Fraunhofer studied the dark lines in sunlight, from 1814. Ångström first observed hydrogen's spectrum, in 1853.

choices.text: Isaac Newton
choices.why: Newton split sunlight into its colors with a prism in 1666. He did not observe hydrogen's line spectrum.

explanation: Anders Ångström first observed the spectrum of hydrogen atoms in Uppsala, Sweden, in 1853. He measured the four visible lines, at 656.21, 486.07, 434.01 and 410.12 nm, that Balmer later fitted with his formula.

prompt: How did Fraunhofer label the strongest dark lines he found in the solar spectrum?

choices.text: With the letters A through K
With the names of the elements causing them
choices.why: The causes were not known then. Fraunhofer labeled the lines with letters; Table 1.4.1 also lists the elements now linked to them.

choices.text: With the numbers 1 to 600
choices.why: He found nearly 600 lines, but he labeled the principal ones with the letters A to K.

choices.text: With the Greek letters α, β, γ, …
choices.why: Greek letters name the lines within a hydrogen series, such as Hα. Fraunhofer used the letters A to K.

explanation: Between 1814 and 1823 Fraunhofer found nearly 600 dark lines in sunlight. He labeled the principal ones with the letters A through K and weaker ones with other letters, as in Table 1.4.1 (for example, the sodium D lines).

prompt: Why does a cool gas between a bright source and a detector produce a dark line in the spectrum?

choices.text: It absorbs light of that frequency and sends it off in other directions or turns it into heat
It reflects the light of every color straight back toward the source
choices.why: The gas removes only narrow bands of frequency, which is why the dark lines are thin.

choices.text: It changes light of that frequency into another color that still reaches the detector
choices.why: The absorbed light is re-emitted mostly in other directions, or turned into heat, so less of it reaches the detector.

choices.text: It blocks all frequencies equally, so the whole spectrum gets darker
choices.why: Only certain narrow frequencies are absorbed, so you see thin dark lines, not an overall dimming.

explanation: Photons of that frequency are absorbed by the gas and then re-emitted in random directions, mostly different from the original one, or turned into heat. So less light in that narrow frequency band reaches the detector, which sees a dark absorption line.

prompt: According to Table 1.4.1, which element is responsible for the Fraunhofer D1 and D2 lines, near 589 nm?

choices.text: Sodium
Hydrogen
choices.why: Hydrogen gives the C line, at 656.281 nm. The D1 and D2 lines come from sodium.

choices.text: Oxygen
choices.why: Oxygen (O2) gives the A, B, a, Z and y lines. The D1 and D2 lines come from sodium.

choices.text: Helium
choices.why: Helium gives the nearby D3 line, at 587.5618 nm. The D1 and D2 lines come from sodium.

explanation: Table 1.4.1 lists D1 (589.592 nm) and D2 (588.995 nm) as sodium lines. Helium gives the nearby D3 line, hydrogen the C line, and O2 the A and B lines.

prompt: Why can the line spectrum of a glowing gas be used to tell which elements are in it?

choices.text: Each element gives its own characteristic pattern of lines
All elements give the same lines, only brighter or dimmer
choices.why: Different elements give lines at different wavelengths, as the spectra of hydrogen, neon and mercury show.

choices.text: The lines depend only on the gas's temperature
choices.why: That is true of a blackbody's continuous spectrum. A line spectrum depends on which atoms are present.

choices.text: Only hydrogen gives a line spectrum
choices.why: Every element gives lines; neon and mercury, for example, have their own patterns.

explanation: Gases heated to incandescence emit light at a set of sharp wavelengths, and these line spectra are characteristic of the atomic composition of the gas. So the pattern of emission or absorption lines tells which atoms are present.

prompt: Who was Johann Balmer, who found a formula for hydrogen's visible lines?

choices.text: A math and Latin teacher at a girls' school in Switzerland
A Swedish physicist who first measured hydrogen's lines
choices.why: That was Anders Ångström. Balmer worked from Ångström's measurements.

choices.text: A physicist who studied the dark lines in sunlight with many prisms
choices.why: That describes Fraunhofer. Balmer was a schoolteacher in Basel who had done no physics before.

choices.text: An English scientist who split sunlight with a prism
choices.why: That was Isaac Newton, in 1666. Balmer was a math and Latin teacher in Basel.

explanation: Johann Balmer was a math and Latin teacher at a girls' school in Basel, Switzerland. He had done no physics before and made his great discovery when he was almost sixty.

prompt: Why did Balmer look for a pattern in the spectrum of hydrogen rather than of another element?

choices.text: As the lightest atom, it seemed likeliest to be simple
It was the only element whose spectrum had been measured
choices.why: Line spectra of many elements were known, from Bunsen, Kirchhoff and others. Balmer picked hydrogen because it is the lightest atom.

choices.text: Its lines are the brightest of all the lines in sunlight
choices.why: Balmer's reason was simplicity: the lightest atom seemed the most likely to show a simple pattern.

choices.text: It has more spectral lines than any other element known
choices.why: Balmer worked with just four lines. He chose hydrogen because, as the lightest atom, it seemed likely to be simple.

explanation: Balmer reasoned that the lightest atom, hydrogen, was the most likely to show a simple spectral pattern. He concentrated on Ångström's four visible lines and found a formula that fitted them.

prompt: Balmer's formula fitted four visible lines, with n_2 = 3, 4, 5 and 6. What did it predict beyond them?

choices.text: More lines at shorter wavelengths, for n_2 = 7, 8, 9, …
No more lines: the four visible lines were the whole series
choices.why: n_2 can keep increasing, and Balmer predicted more lines for n_2 ≥ 7. Some had already been observed.

choices.text: More lines at longer wavelengths, beyond the red line
choices.why: The red line, n_2 = 3, has the longest wavelength in the series. Larger n_2 gives shorter wavelengths.

choices.text: Lines whose wavelengths change with the gas's temperature
choices.why: Balmer's formula has no temperature in it: each n_2 gives one fixed wavelength.

explanation: Balmer predicted further lines for n_2 ≥ 7, at shorter wavelengths toward and into the ultraviolet. Some of them had in fact already been observed, unknown to Balmer; Table 1.4.2 lists them at 397, 389, 383 and 380 nm.

prompt: Balmer guessed that the 4 in his formula could be replaced by 9, 16, 25, …. In which region of the spectrum did the lines this predicts turn up?

choices.text: The infrared
The visible, between the red and teal lines
choices.why: No new visible lines turned up there. The lines from replacing 4 with 9, 16, 25, … are further into the infrared.

choices.text: The ultraviolet
choices.why: The extra Balmer lines (n_2 ≥ 7) head toward the ultraviolet, but the lines from replacing 4 with 9, 16, 25, … are in the infrared.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the guess was wrong
choices.why: The guess turned out to be true, though the lines were not detected until the early twentieth century.

explanation: Balmer's conjecture that the 4 could be replaced by 9, 16, 25, … turned out to be true, but these lines, further into the infrared, were not detected until the early twentieth century.

prompt: In the Balmer series, how does the spacing between neighboring lines change as n_2 increases?

choices.text: It shrinks, so the lines crowd together toward a limit
It grows, so the lines spread farther apart
choices.why: Table 1.4.2 shows the opposite: 656 to 486 nm is a big gap, but 383 to 380 nm is tiny.

choices.text: It stays the same, so the lines are evenly spaced
choices.why: The gaps keep getting smaller, from 170 nm between the first two lines to 3 nm between n_2 = 9 and 10.

choices.text: It alternates between wide and narrow gaps
choices.why: The gaps shrink steadily as n_2 increases, as the lines converge on a highest possible energy.

explanation: As n_2 increases, the energy (and frequency) of the lines rises, but the difference between successive lines decreases. The lines crowd together and converge on a highest possible energy, the limit of the series.

prompt: In the Balmer series, what happens to the wavelength of the line as n_2 increases from 3 to 4 to 5?

choices.text: It gets shorter
It gets longer
choices.why: Table 1.4.2 gives 656, 486 and 434 nm for n_2 = 3, 4 and 5: the wavelength falls.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Each n_2 gives a different line; the wavelength falls from 656 nm to 486 nm to 434 nm.

choices.text: It goes up and down with no pattern
choices.why: The pattern is regular: the wavelength falls steadily as n_2 increases, while the energy rises.

explanation: Table 1.4.2 gives 656 nm (red), 486 nm (teal) and 434 nm (blue) for n_2 = 3, 4 and 5. A larger n_2 gives a shorter wavelength, which means a higher frequency and energy.

prompt: As n_2 gets very large, what value does the wavelength of the Balmer lines approach?

choices.text: About 364.5 nm, the constant b in Balmer's formula
656 nm, the wavelength of the red line
choices.why: 656 nm is the longest Balmer wavelength (n_2 = 3). The wavelengths fall toward 364.5 nm as n_2 grows.

choices.text: 410 nm, the wavelength of the indigo line
choices.why: 410 nm (n_2 = 6) is the last of Ångström's four visible lines, but more lines follow at shorter wavelengths, down to 364.5 nm.

choices.text: Zero, since the lines go on forever
choices.why: The lines do go on, but they crowd together and converge on the series limit, 364.5 nm.

explanation: For very large n_2, n_2^2/(n_2^2 − 4) gets very close to 1, so λ approaches b = 364.56 nm. Example 1.4.1 finds the same limit, 364.5 nm, from the greatest wavenumber, R_H/4 = 27,434 cm^−1.

prompt: According to Table 1.4.2, which of these Balmer lines is not visible to the eye?

choices.why: Table 1.4.2 lists the 397 nm line as violet, so it is visible. The lines from n_2 = 8 on are not.
Table 1.4.2 lists the 410 nm line as indigo, so it is visible. The lines from n_2 = 8 on are not.
Table 1.4.2 lists the 486 nm line as teal, so it is visible. The lines from n_2 = 8 on are not.

explanation: Table 1.4.2 gives colors for n_2 = 3 to 7: red, teal, blue, indigo and violet. The lines for n_2 = 8, 9 and 10, at 389, 383 and 380 nm, are marked not visible.

prompt: Why is the Balmer series particularly useful in astronomy?

choices.text: Hydrogen is so abundant that its Balmer lines are strong in many stars
Balmer lines are the only lines that reach Earth from space
choices.why: Other lines reach Earth too, such as the sodium D lines in sunlight. The Balmer lines are useful because hydrogen is so abundant.

choices.text: Stars contain no element other than hydrogen
choices.why: Stars contain other elements too, but hydrogen is the most abundant, so its lines are common and strong.

choices.text: The Balmer lines are all radio waves, which pass through dust
choices.why: Several Balmer lines are visible light. Their usefulness comes from hydrogen's abundance in the universe.

explanation: Because hydrogen is so abundant in the universe, the Balmer lines appear in numerous stellar objects and are relatively strong compared with lines from other elements.

prompt: Using λν = c, what happens to the wavelength of light if its frequency is doubled?

choices.text: It is halved
It doubles
choices.why: λ and ν are inversely related: their product is fixed at c, so if ν doubles, λ must halve.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Since λν = c and c is constant, changing ν must change λ.

choices.text: It becomes four times shorter
choices.why: That would need a square law. λ = c/ν, so doubling ν halves λ.

explanation: λν = c, and the speed of light c is constant, so wavelength and frequency are inversely proportional: doubling ν halves λ.

prompt: Light has a frequency of 6.00 × 10^14 Hz. Use λ = c/ν with c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s, and 1 nm = 10^−9 m. What is its wavelength, in nm?
A spectral line has a wavenumber of ν̃ = 25,000 cm^−1. Use λ = 1/ν̃ and 1 cm = 10^7 nm. What is its wavelength, in nm?
Use E = hcν̃. Line A has a wavenumber of 30,000 cm^−1 and line B has 15,000 cm^−1. How many times more energy does one photon of line A carry than one photon of line B?
explanation: E_A/E_B = (hcν̃_A)/(hcν̃_B) = (30,000 cm^−1)/(15,000 cm^−1) = 2. Since h and c cancel, the photon energies are in the same ratio as the wavenumbers.
